We have a mass spectrum with peaks at m/z values and intensities. Need to identify elements based on isotope distribution patterns visible. Look at pattern: main peak at 276.0666 intensity 100. Next at 277.0697 intensity ~16% (16% of base). Next at 278.0640 intensity ~33.6% (higher than 277). That's unusual. Typically chlorine shows M+2 ~33% of M, bromine M+2 ~65% of M. Sulfur has M+2 ~4%? Actually 34S ~4.2% relative to 32S. Carbon 13C gives M+1 ~1.1% per carbon. Here we have M+1 (277) 16% suggests many carbons (approx 16%/1.1% ≈ 14-15 carbons). M+2 (278) 33.6% could be combination of 2 13C (2*1.1% per carbon? Actually probability of two 13C ~ (n*1.1%)^2? Not linear). But also presence of chlorine would give M+2 ~33% of M. So chlorine could be present. Also bromine would give M+2 ~65% which is not observed. So chlorine likely. Also sulfur would give M+2 ~4% not 33%. So chlorine is strong candidate.

Also pattern of M+1 16% suggests many carbons, but that doesn't identify element definitively; carbon is always present in organics but not definitive. The question: "list all elements that can be definitively identified" based on isotope distribution patterns visible. Definite identification: chlorine (due to ~33% M+2). Possibly also carbon? But carbon isotopic pattern is not distinctive enough to be definitive unless you see a pattern of many M+1 peaks? Usually you can't definitively say carbon present just from isotopic pattern because many elements have M+1 contributions. However, the presence of a strong M+1 peak could indicate many carbons but not definitive. The question likely expects chlorine as the only element that can be definitively identified from the pattern. Also maybe bromine? Not present. Sulfur not. So answer list: ['Cl'].

Check if any other element shows pattern: maybe chlorine has two isotopes 35Cl (75.78%) and 37Cl (24.22%) giving M+2 ~32% of M. That matches. So answer.

Thus final answer list.
